title: Counterfeit Component Detection - Methods That Actually Work
summary: The broker market can be an extremely useful source of components, especially when authorized distribution comes up empty. Plenty of independent distributors do an excellent job of supplying legitimate inventory, and a supplier that's earned your trust can save you considerable testing expense.

##


Those components might work perfectly and still be counterfeit. They could have been pulled off scrap circuit boards, cleaned up, and repackaged to look brand new. And once they're soldered onto your boards, figuring out that you've bought somebody else's used chips gets considerably more expensive.


Unfortunately, buying from independent distributors, aka 'brokers', is sometimes unavoidable, especially when you're dealing with shortages, obsolete components, or production deadlines that aren't particularly interested in your sourcing problems.


The good news is that you can substantially reduce your risk without becoming a counterfeit semiconductor investigator. You just need to know which suppliers deserve your trust, when testing is necessary, and what to ask the testing laboratory to actually do.


We'll walk through how to evaluate brokers, when you can reasonably accept factory-sealed inventory without additional testing, and which counterfeit inspection methods are worth paying for. We'll also explain why some commonly offered tests provide considerably less protection than their impressive-sounding names suggest.


## The Best Counterfeit Prevention Strategy Is Authorized Sourcing


The simplest way to avoid counterfeit electronic components is to buy them directly from the original component manufacturer (OCM) or an authorized distributor.


Companies like DigiKey, Mouser, Arrow, and Avnet have established relationships with the manufacturers whose components they sell. Assuming the parts have stayed within that authorized supply chain, you have good reason to believe you're receiving genuine, new components. NASA's[electronic parts-assurance guidance](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/NASA/NASA-STD-873910) recognizes the lower risk associated with authorized sourcing.


Ideally, you'd buy everything this way and never have to think about counterfeit inspections.


Unfortunately, components go obsolete, manufacturers experience shortages, and sometimes an authorized distributor quotes a lead time that's longer than your entire product development schedule.


That's when brokers become extremely useful.


There are plenty of reputable brokers supplying legitimate components every day. The challenge is figuring out which suppliers you can trust and what precautions to take when you're dealing with someone unfamiliar.


## What Does Counterfeit Mean in Electronic Components?


When most people hear "counterfeit", they picture a completely fake product. A chip with somebody else's silicon inside and a manufacturer's logo printed on top certainly qualifies, although the electronics industry has a considerably broader counterfeit definition.


When we're evaluating electronic components, the practical definition of counterfeit is parts that are *not* both new and original.


"New" means the components have never been used, reclaimed, refurbished, or remarked. A semiconductor that spent five years operating inside an industrial controller before somebody removed it and cleaned it up doesn't qualify, even if it still works beautifully.


"Original" means the component contains the genuine manufacturer's die, which is the actual silicon chip inside the package, corresponding to the part number you ordered.


These are separate things to verify because it's entirely possible to have an original component that's been used or a brand-new-looking component containing the wrong die.


[Formal counterfeit definitions](https://www.acquisition.gov/dfars/252.246-7007-contractor-counterfeit-electronic-part-detection-and-avoidance-system.) also include unauthorized substitutions, altered date codes, misrepresented performance grades, and other deliberate misrepresentations of component identity or condition.

## When Can You Trust a Broker Without Additional Counterfeit Testing?


### What Is a Trusted Broker?


Your best indicator of whether a broker is trustworthy is often your own purchasing history.


When you've bought components from a supplier repeatedly, received exactly what you ordered, and seen them handle problems professionally, you've developed a meaningful basis for trust.


Of course, that doesn't help much when you're buying from someone for the first time.


Industry reputation and references are useful starting points. A good reference is established industry distributor rankings, such as[Supply Chain Connect's 2026 Top 25 North American Independent Distributors](https://www.supplychainconnect.com/rankings-research/article/55376781/2026-top-25-independent-electronics-distributors-list) .


Those rankings provide some evidence that a company is an established participant in the industry. You'll still need to assess its inspection procedures and business practices.


Another particularly useful indicator is membership in[ERAI](https://www.erai.com/membership_options_erai_member.aspx) , an organization focused on counterfeit-component and supplier risk.


ERAI requires prospective supplier members to meet certain business-verification requirements, provide at least ten verifiable trade references, and have no unresolved complaints listed with ERAI at the time of application.


There's a small trick worth knowing here. ERAI provides a clickable Smart Logo that verifies a supplier's membership status. If you see an ERAI logo on a broker's website, click it and check that the linked membership information matches the supplier. A picture of a logo is pretty easy to copy.


None of these indicators guarantees that every component a supplier sells will be authentic. You'll need to make your own judgment, although they're useful evidence when deciding how much inspection to require.


### Buying Factory-Sealed Components From a Trusted Broker


When a trusted broker offers components in original, factory-sealed packaging, you can generally be comfortable approving the purchase without additional counterfeit testing.


You should still require a written guarantee that the components are new and original, along with a warranty. One year is a customary warranty period for trusted, credible brokers.


Factory-sealed inventory has a particular advantage. The original sealed packaging provides strong evidence the parts are new and original, and opening it for inspection means sacrificing that evidence.


There's little benefit in paying someone to break open a perfectly good factory-sealed reel when you have good reason to trust the supplier and the material.


Documentation establishing an unbroken chain of custody back to the manufacturer would give you even greater confidence, although that level of traceability is uncommon in the broker market and can command a significant premium.


One caution: counterfeiters can reproduce factory packaging and seals quite convincingly. A beautifully sealed bag from a broker you've never dealt with deserves real scrutiny.


### Buying Open-Box Components From a Trusted Broker


Things change somewhat when the broker is selling open-box inventory, partial reels, cut tape, or components that have otherwise been removed from their original packaging.


A trusted broker should have established inspection procedures and access to appropriate testing equipment. There's generally no reason to insist on an outside laboratory if you have confidence in the broker's processes and capabilities.


You should, however, understand what those processes include. We'll get into the actual testing methods shortly, so you'll have a reasonable basis for judging whether a supplier's inspection program is adequate.


## What Should You Require From an Untrusted Broker?


### Require Counterfeit Testing and a New-and-Original Warranty


Suppose you've located exactly the parts you need, but the supplier is unfamiliar and you haven't found enough evidence to consider them trustworthy.


Before placing the order, insist that the broker guarantee the components are new and original.


Prefer a one-year warranty, although three months is generally reasonable. A supplier offering less than three months deserves closer scrutiny, especially if it's already difficult to establish where the material originated.


You also need to specify the counterfeit testing requirements before placing the order.


A broker may advertise "100% tested" inventory, which sounds fantastic until you learn that the testing consists of a quick visual examination or a basic functionality check.


Ask which inspections will be performed, how many components will be examined, and require your approval of the actual test results before shipment.


A certificate stating that the parts passed inspection gives you considerably less information than photographs, X-ray images, measurements, and documented findings.


[SAE AS6081A](https://saemobilus.sae.org/standards/as6081a-counterfeit-electrical-electronic-electromechanical-eee-parts-avoidance-detection-mitigation-disposition-independent-distribution) provides an industry standard for counterfeit avoidance and detection practices in independent distribution.


### Should You Allow the Broker to Conduct the Tests?


Sometimes you'll encounter a broker that appears credible but hasn't yet earned your complete confidence.


This is a reasonable situation for a trust-but-verify approach.


You can allow the broker to perform its own counterfeit inspections, provided you've agreed on the tests beforehand and can review the underlying evidence.


Require your approval of the test results before the material ships. That gives you an opportunity to question anything suspicious while the broker still has possession of the components.


The sections below will help you determine which tests to request.


### When Should You Require a Third-Party Laboratory?


When you're dealing with an unfamiliar broker that hasn't established its credibility, the default recommendation is independent laboratory inspection.


You should select a reputable laboratory with the appropriate capabilities, ideally one that works to the relevant SAE AS6171 test methods. SAE AS6810 addresses laboratory accreditation for these counterfeit-detection methods.


The purchase agreement should spell out that the broker must ship the material directly to the agreed laboratory for inspection before you accept delivery or take possession.


The laboratory should perform the specified tests, provide you with a complete report, and confirm whether the inspected material meets the agreed acceptance criteria.


If the components fail, the agreement should permit rejection without requiring you to accept the shipment. Arrange for the laboratory to return rejected material directly to the supplier where applicable law and counterfeit-handling requirements permit.


This arrangement protects you from a rather unpleasant scenario in which you've already paid for questionable components and are now trying to persuade a broker on the other side of the world to take them back.


Speaking of the other side of the world, when you're sourcing components from Asia, there's often a good reason to use a qualified laboratory located in Asia. Shipping parts halfway around the planet for testing, then sending them back again, adds transportation expense and delay.


There's another benefit to requiring independent testing that deserves some attention.


A reputable broker should be comfortable with the idea of having its inventory inspected, even if the supplier wants to negotiate who pays for the testing.


Occasionally, a broker that seemed very enthusiastic about selling you components will suddenly announce that the material is unavailable as soon as you mention independent laboratory inspection.


Consider that a pretty successful counterfeit avoidance exercise. You've potentially avoided a bad purchase without spending a dime on laboratory testing.


### Consider Using an Escrow Service


An escrow service can give you additional financial protection when buying from an unfamiliar supplier.


Essentially, escrow means an independent intermediary holds your payment until the conditions you've agreed upon with the seller have been satisfied.


You and the broker agree on the inspection requirements, acceptance criteria, and payment-release conditions before the transaction proceeds. The escrow provider then releases payment according to those agreed terms.


A few services specialize in the electronics industry:


- [ERAI's eraiESCROW](https://www.eraiescrow.com/) allows buyers to inspect and test material before payment is released.
- [The Broker Forum's Escrow Plus](https://marketing.brokerforum.com/escrow/html/Works.html) includes options for independent laboratory inspection and pass/fail acceptance conditions.
- [HK Inventory's escrow service](https://www1.hkinventory.com/public/EscrowService.asp) offers transaction protection with an agreed inspection period.


Check each service's current eligibility requirements, fees, and terms. The cost is typically around 1% of the transaction value.


A broker's willingness to use escrow is another encouraging indicator of the brokers credibility.


## Recommended Tests for "New"


Now that we've covered who should be testing your components, we can get into what they should actually be testing.


There are several techniques commonly used in counterfeit inspection, and each one tells you something different about the parts.


Let's start with determining whether the components are genuinely new.


### External Visual Inspection (EVI): Has the Component Been Used?


External visual inspection is the basic starting point for evaluating unsealed electronic components.


An experienced inspector examines the component markings, date codes, packaging, labels, and physical condition, generally using magnification.


They're looking for evidence that the part has been previously handled, altered, or installed on a circuit board.


Scratches, unusual surface textures, inconsistent markings, solder residue, and evidence of resurfacing or blacktopping can all indicate problems. SAE AS6171/2A describes the relevant inspection methods.


One particularly useful technique is examining the leads.


Many components have leads that are plated before they're trimmed to their finished length. The freshly cut ends therefore expose copper beneath the plating.


If those ends have subsequently been coated with solder or another finish, that's suspicious because the component may have been replated after removal from a circuit board.


There are legitimate manufacturing variations to account for, so exposed copper alone doesn't prove newness. However, the absence of exposed copper when it should be present will almost always result in a 'not new' determination.


For unsealed components, external visual inspection should be part of your baseline testing requirements.


Read More:[The Easiest Way to Spot Counterfeit Electronic Components](https://www.cofactr.com/articles/the-easiest-way-to-spot-counterfeit-electronic-components)


### Heated Chemical Testing (HCT): Has the Component Been Remarked?


One popular counterfeiting technique involves removing the original markings from a semiconductor package, applying a fresh surface coating, and printing whatever part number the counterfeiter wants to sell.


This process is commonly called remarking or blacktopping.


Basic counterfeit inspections may include wiping the package with acetone or alcohol, sometimes accompanied by a scrape test.


Those techniques can reveal crude attempts at remarking, although they're subjective and can miss more sophisticated resurfacing work.


A component that survives a quick acetone wipe may still have somebody else's part number hiding underneath a coating that's resistant to the solvent.


Heated chemical testing uses an appropriate controlled chemical procedure to examine whether markings or surface coatings have been altered. When the package material and applicable method permit it, this is a stronger option for detecting sophisticated resurfacing.


Specify appropriate heated chemical testing for questionable unsealed components, with the laboratory determining which procedure is compatible with the package.


## Recommended Tests for "Original"


Most inspection sequences begin with the tests for newness. In most cases, if the parts are found to be not-new, you should stop inspecting further and reject the parts.


Once you've established that the semiconductor looks legitimate, we now need to consider what's inside.


This is where X-ray inspection and decapsulation become particularly valuable.


### X-Ray Inspection: Does the Component Contain the Expected Die?


X-ray inspection allows you to examine the internal construction of a semiconductor without opening its package.


An X-ray image can reveal whether a die is present, how large it is, where it's positioned, and how the bond wires connect it to the package leads.


If you have a known-good component for comparison, you can look for differences in die dimensions, wire-bond arrangements, and other internal structures.


Suppose you order an expensive microcontroller and discover that the die inside is substantially smaller than the one found in a known-good example. That's the kind of discrepancy that deserves serious investigation.


[SAE AS6171/5](https://saemobilus.sae.org/standards/as61715-techniques-suspect-counterfeit-eee-parts-detection-radiological-test-methods) covers radiological inspection techniques.


We strongly recommend X-ray inspection when buying unsealed packaged semiconductors through untrusted brokers.


The limitation is that X-ray generally can't read the markings on the silicon itself. Two different devices can have similar internal construction, and a reclaimed genuine chip may produce exactly the X-ray image you'd expect.


GAO investigations have documented suspect counterfeit components that passed radiological inspection before other methods exposed evidence of misrepresentation.


Read More:[X-Ray Inspection for Counterfeits: When You Need It (and When You Don't)](https://www.cofactr.com/articles/x-ray-inspection-for-counterfeits-when-you-need-it-and-when-you-dont)


### Decapsulation (Decap): Is It the Manufacturer's Original Die?


Decapsulation is where we get to open the package and look directly at the silicon.


The laboratory removes enough of the encapsulating material to expose the die, which can then be inspected for manufacturer identifiers, die markings, layout, and other distinguishing characteristics.


This gives you much stronger evidence about the chip's identity than you can obtain from an X-ray image alone. SAE AS6171/4 describes the relevant physical analysis methods.


Generally, favor of decap for questionable semiconductor lots, especially expensive or high-risk components.


There is one rather obvious disadvantage. Once you've chemically opened a semiconductor package, that component isn't going into your finished product.


If you're purchasing ten obsolete processors and each one costs $800, you may have understandable reservations about sacrificing one to the testing laboratory.


You also need to consider sampling. Opening two components and finding genuine dies provides useful evidence about those samples, although the remaining material could still contain substituted parts.


### X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF): Does the Material Composition Match?


X-ray fluorescence, generally called XRF, measures the elemental composition of materials.


For electronic components, it's particularly useful for checking the composition of lead finishes and identifying discrepancies between the expected and actual metallurgy.


For example, a component sold with a particular leaded finish might turn out to have a lead-free finish instead.


XRF helped identify material inconsistencies in GAO investigations of suspect counterfeit components.


It's a useful additional test when you suspect refinishing, material substitution, or an incorrect component grade. You shouldn't routinely insist on XRF for every broker purchase unless the material or reliability requirements justify it.


## When Should You Require Additional Electrical and Manufacturing Tests?


There are a couple of other testing categories worth discussing because they address problems that counterfeit inspection alone may leave unresolved.


### Electrical Testing: Does the Component Meet Its Specifications?


Electrical testing tells you whether a component performs according to specified electrical requirements.


Depending on the device, this might include DC parameters such as leakage current and supply current, along with AC specifications such as propagation delay, switching characteristics, or maximum operating frequency.


For an analog component, you might care about offset voltage, gain, bandwidth, or other performance characteristics.[SAE AS6171/7](https://saemobilus.sae.org/standards/as61717-techniques-suspect-counterfeit-eee-parts-detection-electrical-test-methods) covers electrical testing methods used in counterfeit investigations.


The particular tests matter enormously.


Checking that a microcontroller powers on and executes a simple program gives you a very limited view of its performance.


Testing more of the actual datasheet requirements, especially specifications relevant to your application, can expose incorrect grades, degraded components, and substituted devices.


You might test a sample from the lot or specify 100% testing when the failure consequences justify the expense.


Just keep in mind that a counterfeit component can pass extensive electrical testing.


A genuine chip reclaimed from a scrap circuit board may function perfectly today. Its previous thermal exposure, operating history, and remaining useful life are still unknown.


### Coplanarity and Solderability Testing: Will the Components Assemble Correctly?


Older components deserve some additional attention, even when they're new and original.


Inventory with date codes more than three to five years old is a reasonable candidate for extra manufacturing-readiness checks, especially when its storage history is unclear.


Coplanarity testing examines whether leads or terminals are properly aligned. Bent or uneven leads can create problems during assembly.


Solderability testing checks whether the component terminations can form acceptable solder joints.


Poor storage conditions, oxidation, or degraded finishes can make otherwise legitimate inventory difficult to assemble reliably.


Neither test authenticates the silicon. They help you avoid discovering assembly problems after the components arrive at your contract manufacturer, when you're already under pressure to get boards built.


## A Major Warning Sign: Brokers Who Guarantee Only Functionality


There's one particular situation where I'd recommend being extremely cautious.


Sometimes a broker will happily tell you that the components are tested and guaranteed functional but refuse to guarantee that they're new and original.


That should make you nervous.


It may mean the broker doesn't actually own the inventory and has limited visibility into its origin. Perhaps the material is being offered by another supplier several steps removed from whoever originally acquired it.


It could also mean the broker knows something about the components that makes a new-and-original guarantee uncomfortable.


Whatever the reason, a supplier that refuses to stand behind the identity and condition of the material is asking you to accept some substantial unknowns.


You should absolutely walk away from these transactions.


## What If You Have No Alternative?


Occasionally, the component you need is obsolete, the production schedule is unforgiving, and a supplier offering a functionality-only guarantee has the only inventory you can locate.


At that point, you have a deliberate risk decision to make.


Start by determining whether your product and any applicable contractual or regulatory requirements permit the use of components whose origin or previous service history cannot be established.


If proceeding is permissible, it is strongly recommend to use an escrow service so payment is tied to agreed inspection and acceptance requirements.


Also, pay considerably more attention to electrical characterization. Have the laboratory verify the AC and DC parameters most relevant to your application, and consider 100% electrical testing if failures would be particularly expensive or dangerous.


Solderability and coplanarity testing may be appropriate, especially for older stock. External inspection, X-ray, and decap can still provide valuable information about the condition and identity of the material.


You'll need to accept that some uncertainty will remain. A component may pass every specified test today while still carrying unknown damage or reduced remaining service life from its previous use.

## Understand Counterfeit Testing Before You Buy


The broker market can be an extremely useful source of components, especially when authorized distribution comes up empty. Plenty of independent distributors do an excellent job of supplying legitimate inventory, and a supplier that's earned your trust can save you considerable testing expense.


When you're dealing with unfamiliar suppliers, though, it's worth spending some time getting the purchase terms right before you send money.


Require a new-and-original guarantee, specify inspections that address the actual risks, and arrange for independent testing when the supplier hasn't earned your confidence.


If the broker refuses reasonable inspection requirements or suddenly loses interest in selling you the material, count yourself lucky. There's something satisfying about avoiding a counterfeit-component problem before the components ever reaches your loading dock.

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What are counterfeit electronic components?**


Counterfeit electronic components are parts misrepresented as new or original. They may contain incorrect semiconductor dies, altered markings, unauthorized substitutions, or previously used components sold as new.


**How can I avoid buying counterfeit electronic components?**


Purchase components directly from original manufacturers or authorized distributors such as DigiKey, Mouser, Arrow, and Avnet. When using brokers, verify supplier credibility and establish appropriate inspection requirements.


**What is the best way to verify an electronic component broker?**


Review previous purchasing experience, industry references, ERAI membership, and inspection capabilities. Established distributor rankings provide additional evidence, although no single credential guarantees component authenticity.


**Can I buy factory-sealed electronic components without counterfeit testing?**


Yes, factory-sealed components from trusted brokers generally require no additional counterfeit testing. Obtain a written new-and-original guarantee and warranty, preferably covering one year, before purchasing the inventory.


**When should I require third-party counterfeit component testing?**


Require independent laboratory inspection when purchasing from unfamiliar brokers with unverified credibility. Specify testing requirements, acceptance criteria, and shipment procedures before placing the order or accepting delivery.


**How does external visual inspection identify counterfeit electronic components?**


External visual inspection examines component markings, date codes, packaging, surface textures, and leads. Inspectors look for solder residue, resurfacing, inconsistent markings, and other evidence of previous use.


**What is heated chemical testing for electronic components?**


Heated chemical testing uses controlled chemical procedures to detect altered package surfaces and markings. It can identify sophisticated resurfacing or blacktopping that basic solvent wipes might miss.


**Why does X-ray inspection help detect counterfeit semiconductors?**


X-ray inspection reveals internal semiconductor structures, including die dimensions, placement, and bond-wire connections. Comparing these features against known-good components can expose substitutions or suspicious manufacturing differences.


**Is decapsulation testing necessary for counterfeit semiconductor detection?**


Decapsulation provides stronger evidence of semiconductor identity by exposing the die for direct examination. It is particularly valuable for questionable, expensive, or high-risk components, although testing destroys samples.


**When does older electronic component inventory require additional testing?**


Components with date codes older than three to five years may need solderability and coplanarity testing, particularly when storage conditions are unknown or assembly reliability matters.


**Should I buy electronic components from brokers offering only functionality guarantees?**


Generally, avoid suppliers unwilling to guarantee components are new and original. Functional testing cannot establish previous service history, remaining useful life, or authenticity, even when devices operate correctly.
